children: Asset managers are selling long-duration U.S. Treasury futures contracts, suggesting forced selling is emerging as cash yields hover near multi-year highs. According to Sina Finance, CFTC data showed that over the two weeks through October 6, asset managers cut their net long positions in ultra-long Treasury futures by about $27 million per basis point of risk, equivalent to roughly $38 billion of current benchmark 10-year U.S. Treasury cash bonds.

During the same period, Treasury futures prices fell sharply as the 30-year U.S. Treasury yield rose to a 24-year high of 5.68%. The move is part of a months-long Treasury selloff driven by market concerns over the inflation impact of U.S. and Israeli strikes on Iran, deteriorating global government finances, and the U.S. economy that the Federal Reserve is trying to restrain amid the AI boom.

According to Sina Finance, the latest CFTC data released on Friday also showed that technical factors are intensifying the recent decline in long-dated Treasuries. Asset managers showed signs of forced selling after the cheapest-to-deliver mechanism lengthened portfolio duration.

The so-called switch risk is triggered when the deliverable basket changes and the cheapest-to-deliver bond shifts toward longer maturities, which can force selling. Open interest also confirmed the deleveraging in ultra-long Treasury futures, with open interest falling for seven straight trading days and cumulative risk reduction reaching nearly $20 million per basis point. Rising yields over the same period also indicated that long positions were being unwound.

title: US Treasury Futures See Forced Selling Signs as Asset Managers Deleverage
